abstract: >-
  Most EEG source imaging methods assume brain activity arises from independent, focal sources and are validated mainly on their ability to localize a single generator — overlooking the brain's network structure and the propagation of activity along it. We introduce weighted Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (wCSET), which replaces its predecessor CSET's L1 sparsity prior with a smooth, exponentially weighted L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum. We validate wCSET, CSET, three standard connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based (Laplace-Beltrami) alternative across three complementary studies that probe source reconstruction beyond localization: simulated activity propagating across a structural connectome, providing an exact network-level ground truth; a clinical cohort of 26 seizure-free epilepsy patients, using the resected epileptogenic zone as ground truth; and simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG recordings, a rare direct electrophysiological benchmark. In simulation, wCSET matched standard methods at localizing a source's onset but substantially outperformed them at reconstructing its subsequent propagation, an advantage robust to noise and to considerable connectome corruption. In the resection cohort, wCSET preserved localization accuracy while requiring markedly less reconstructed cortex to reach the true epileptogenic zone than any competitor. Against intracranial recordings, wCSET outperformed standard and connectivity-agnostic methods in one of two evaluable subjects, but was itself outperformed by a purely geometric alternative in both — suggesting cortical geometry alone may capture much of what drives accurate distributed reconstruction. Together, these results establish wCSET as a principled step beyond localization-only source imaging, and introduce a validation framework for evaluating such methods against a source's full activity pattern rather than its location alone.

# Introduction

Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely utilized for its unparalleled temporal resolution, which allows researchers to study neural dynamics _in vivo_. However, as measurements are primarily recorded at the scalp, the technique suffers from poor spatial resolution [@nunez_electric_2006]. In 1993, the Minimum Norm Estimate (MNE) was introduced to project EEG data onto a cortical surface modeled from individual MRI [@dale_improved_1993]. This approach, broadly termed source reconstruction, aimed to combine the high temporal resolution of EEG with the spatial precision of structural imaging.

Despite three decades of evolution into a diverse array of variants (e.g., sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002], eLORETA [@pascual-marqui_discrete_2007], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], LCMV [@van_veen_localization_1997]), these methods are still primarily used to identify isolated brain regions — a practice often called source localization [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. This focus on localization overlooks a fundamental shift in modern neuroscience toward connectomics. As the "localizationist" view reaches its theoretical limits, it is being superseded by connectivity neuroscience, which treats the brain as an integrated system of interacting networks rather than a collection of independent regions [@bressler_large-scale_2010].

Widely used source reconstruction methods — such as sLORETA, eLORETA, dSPM, and LCMV — remain largely ill-suited for this shift because they rely on the assumption of independent sources, a prior known to perform worse than one informed by the true source covariance structure [@wipf_unified_2009]. This assumption is defensible when activity is genuinely focal — for example, identifying the cortical onset of a sensory stimulus or an epileptic spike — but breaks down as soon as multiple brain regions are simultaneously involved. Because the EEG inverse problem is fundamentally ill-posed due to volume conduction, reconstructed activity from interacting sources blurs together across the cortex — a phenomenon @schoffelen_source_2009 calls field spread and others term leakage [@schoffelen_source_2009; @gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018]. A structured prior on source interactions cannot remove this ill-posedness, but, unlike the independent-sources assumption, it can mitigate leakage's impact [@gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018].

Several strategies have been proposed to address this. Some methods incorporate functional priors from fMRI to constrain expected source interactions [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021]; however, this approach is constrained by the mismatch between fMRI's hemodynamic response, which unfolds over seconds, and the millisecond-scale dynamics of EEG source activity, limiting how precisely such a prior can constrain the interactions it is meant to inform. Others take an agnostic approach, jointly estimating source activities and their unknown covariance structure from the data itself — a family exemplified by BC-VARETA [@gonzalez-moreira_third_2018], at the cost of greater ill-posedness and computational expense. A third strategy draws on the growing body of evidence for structure–function coupling: since neural activity is known to propagate along the brain's structural scaffolding, the connectome estimated from diffusion MRI tractography provides a principled and subject-specific prior for source reconstruction [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024].

Graph Signal Processing (GSP) provides the mathematical machinery to exploit this coupling [@shuman_emerging_2013]. By applying eigendecomposition to the connectome's graph Laplacian, one obtains an orthonormal set of brain harmonics — eigenvectors ordered by their associated graph frequency [@atasoy_human_2016]. Low-frequency harmonics capture smooth, globally integrated patterns of activity; high-frequency harmonics encode more locally segregated ones [@shuman_emerging_2013; @atasoy_human_2016]. Projecting source activity onto this eigenbasis — the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) — yields a compact representation termed the connectome spectrum. Crucially, recent work has demonstrated that both fMRI and EEG source activity are highly compact in this domain: activity energy concentrates predominantly in low-frequency harmonics and decays following an inverse curve [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021], reflecting the tendency of brain dynamics to align with the smooth, integrative modes of the structural connectome [@atasoy_human_2016]. Rué-Queralt et al. (2024) leveraged this principle to introduce Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET): a source reconstruction method that enforces an L₁ sparsity prior directly in the connectome spectrum, restricting solutions to a small number of active harmonics and thereby embedding structural organisation into the reconstruction.

Similar concepts have been explored using the Beltrami-Laplace operator applied to the cortical mesh rather than the connectome's graph Laplacian [@pang_geometric_2023]. This substitutes white matter tractography with the local geometry of the gray matter surface, capturing fine-grained short-range connectivity at the expense of the long-range structural pathways defined by white matter tracts. Pang et al. (2023) showed that geometric eigenmodes derived this way reconstruct functional brain activity at least as accurately as eigenmodes derived from structural connectomes, indicating that cortical geometry alone can yield spectral representations of neural signals that are comparably compact to connectome-based ones [@pang_geometric_2023]. Building on this, Wang et al. (2026) developed Geometric Basis Functions (GBF), representing whole-brain EEG/MEG activity as a linear combination of the leading ~200 Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical surface (capturing ~87% of cortical variance), regularized by an L₂ penalty whose weight decays logarithmically across eigenvalue-ordered geometric modes [@wang_geometry_2026]. Pok Him Siu et al., by contrast, proposed a weighted spectral method based on SVD truncation of the forward operator: the weighted Beltrami-operator harmonics act as a hard spectral filter applied after source reconstruction — determining which components are retained — rather than as a continuous penalty embedded in the optimization itself [@siu_structural_2026].

So far, CSET has no principled way to distinguish biologically meaningful harmonics from those dominated by noise, unlike the geometry-based methods described above, which weight low-order harmonics preferentially by construction. In this work, we address this with weighted CSET (wCSET), which replaces the L₁ prior with a weighted L₂ prior whose penalties follow an exponential decay on graph frequency — a continuous, eigenvalue-graded penalty in the same spirit as GBF's, but applied to the connectome's graph Laplacian rather than the cortical mesh's Beltrami-Laplace operator, and with a different (exponential rather than logarithmic) decay shape. Such a weighting is well justified by the findings of Abdelnour et al. (2018) [@abdelnour_functional_2018], who show that functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural connectome Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, so that a small number of low-frequency structural eigenmodes dominate functional connectivity. Unlike the geometry-based approaches described above, the graph used here is a connectome that is fully aware of the underlying white matter tracts.

Despite this progression from a fixed L₁ sparsity prior to increasingly principled, geometry- and connectome-informed spectral weightings, a critical gap remains in how these methods have actually been validated. Rué-Queralt et al. validated CSET by correlating reconstructed source activity with fMRI data from the same task. Yet fMRI measures hemodynamic responses — blood oxygenation changes driven by neurovascular coupling — which reflect neural activity only indirectly and with significant temporal blurring. The resulting mismatch between EEG source reconstructions and fMRI extends well beyond what correlation can account for, and constitutes a weak proxy for the electrophysiological ground truth these methods aim to reconstruct. The remaining works validate through source localization in epilepsy patients. While some report improvements in estimated source extent, this evaluation criterion is misaligned with the aim of connectivity-informed methods, which are designed not to refine the spatial footprint of a focal source, but to capture the dynamics of activity across interconnected networks — a capability that localization accuracy does not measure.

The primary barrier to a more appropriate validation is therefore the lack of a ground truth for interconnected neural dynamics. We address this gap on three complementary fronts. First, we simulate activity propagating across the structural connectome itself (Section 2.1.1), which provides an exact, fully known ground truth for network-level dynamics that no empirical recording can offer. Second, in a clinical cohort where the resected epileptogenic zone serves as ground truth, we introduce the Network Concentration Index (Section 2.6.3), a metric that evaluates how tightly reconstructed activity concentrates onto the resection as a whole rather than testing only its single most active vertex, directly probing the distributed sensitivity that connectivity-informed methods are designed to provide. Third, we revive and extend the framework proposed by Grova et al. (2016) [@grova_intracranial_2016], who correlated MEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings from the same patients — extending it here to truly simultaneous EEG and iEEG recordings. Unlike fMRI or localization benchmarks, iEEG directly measures electrical potential within the brain — free from neurovascular coupling, skull attenuation, and temporal blurring [@nunez_electric_2006] — making it the only available electrophysiological ground truth for dynamic source reconstruction. By projecting EEG-reconstructed sources onto iEEG electrode locations, we obtain two directly comparable datasets — estimated iEEG and true iEEG — providing an electrophysiologically grounded benchmark for evaluating source reconstruction beyond localization.

Building on this three-part framework, we evaluate CSET and wCSET across three complementary studies:

- **Study I:** Using simulations of spontaneous source diffusion via dMRI-based structural connectivity, we demonstrate that while standard methods accurately localize a source's _onset_, connectivity-informed methods are significantly superior at capturing its _propagation_. We also assess the robustness of these methods against erroneous connectivity data.

- **Study II:** Using a clinical epilepsy dataset where post-surgical success defines the ground truth, we apply the Network Concentration Index introduced above to show that connectivity-informed methods concentrate reconstructed activity more tightly onto the resected zone than standard methods, while preserving localization accuracy comparable to gold-standard clinical algorithms — confirming that the gain in network sensitivity does not come at the cost of focal precision.

- **Study III:** Using simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings, we validate source reconstruction directly against intracranial measurements, demonstrating the ability of connectivity-informed methods to map dynamic neural networks beyond simple point-source localization.

Together, these studies establish wCSET as a principled and clinically viable tool for reconstructing distributed brain dynamics, and introduce a multi-level validation framework that moves the field beyond localization as the sole benchmark for source imaging.


# Materials and Methods

## Data Acquisition and Datasets

### Synthetic Data

Simulations were conducted using anatomical data from a single representative subject selected from the VEPCON dataset [@pascucci_source_2022]. The anatomical framework consists of a T1-weighted MRI and a corresponding structural tractogram derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). EEG signals were simulated on a 204-channel montage derived from a 256-channel EGI HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net, after removing cheek electrodes. The cortical source space (Section 2.3.1) was parcellated into brain regions using the MultiConn atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022] (~400 regions, 2–10 dipoles per region). To keep the simulation budget tractable while retaining broad cortical coverage, a subset of 100 regions was selected via greedy farthest-point sampling over region centroids, yielding a spatially uniform probe set that is reused across every simulation-based analysis in this study except the noise-robustness analysis (Section 3.1.2): sweeping multiple SNR levels per region across the full 100-region set would have been computationally impractical, so a separate, independently-sampled subset of 50 regions was used there instead. In each simulation trial, a source region was drawn from the relevant probe set, and a spike-like waveform was assigned to all dipoles within that region, following classic simulation approaches in which epileptiform activity is modelled as a patch of simultaneously active dipoles rather than a single point source [@afnan_eegmeg_2024]. The spike waveform is a double Hanning window defined as:

$$
s_0(t) = \begin{cases} h\!\left(t,\, \tfrac{2}{3}W\right) & 0 \leq t \leq \tfrac{2}{3}W \\[4pt] -\tfrac{1}{2}\,h\!\left(t - \tfrac{2}{3}W,\; \tfrac{1}{3}W\right) & \tfrac{2}{3}W < t \leq W \end{cases}
$$

where $h(t, T) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)\right]$ is a Hanning window of duration $T$, and $W = 0.05$ s (50 ms) is the total spike duration, chosen to fall centrally within the consensus clinical EEG duration convention for interictal spikes specifically (20–70 ms) [@kane_revised_2017]. The waveform consists of a dominant positive lobe spanning two-thirds of the spike duration, followed by a half-amplitude negative rebound over the remaining third, mimicking the morphology of a clinical interictal spike <!-- supp fig (spike example)-->. The spike signal is then convolved with a Dirac comb recurring every 1 s into a 20 s simulated recording, to generate a train of 20 spike events at the source level; once propagated across the connectome and projected to the sensors (see below and Section 2.2), these are epoched around each event and averaged in EEG sensor space into a single evoked response per simulated run, mirroring the spike-triggered averaging used to construct the clinical datasets in Studies 2 and 3.

**Propagation model.**
Activity was propagated across the connectome in a feedforward manner. The activity at dipole $j$ was modelled as:

$$
S_j(t) = \gamma^{h_j} \cdot s_0\!\left(t - \tau_j\right)
$$

where $s_0(t)$ is the source waveform, $h_j$ is the number of hops (graph edges) along the shortest path from the source to dipole $j$, and $\gamma \in [0,1]$ is a per-hop spatial decay factor, set to $\gamma = 0.5$: without it, activity would propagate undiminished along every reachable path and spread across the entire connectome, rather than attenuating with network distance from the source as genuine, spatially-bounded propagation should. The total propagation delay $\tau_j$ was computed as the sum of per-edge delays along that path:

$$
\tau_j = \sum_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{P}_j} \!\left(\frac{l_{uv}}{v(l_{uv})} + \tau_p\right) + \epsilon_\tau, \qquad v(l) = \begin{cases} 4.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l > 35 \text{ mm (long-range)} \\ 2.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l \leq 35 \text{ mm (U-fiber)} \end{cases}
$$

where $l_{uv}$ is the fiber length of edge $(u,v)$ in mm, and $v(l_{uv})$ is a conduction speed that depends on fiber length: 4.5 mm/ms for long-range tracts above 35 mm — the central estimate of two independent large-sample cortico-cortical evoked potential (CCEP) studies converging on ~3–6 m/s for adult long-range association fibers [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] — and a slower 2.5 mm/ms for short-range U-fibers at or below 35 mm, reflecting their distinctly slower reported conduction (~2–3 m/s) relative to long-range tracts [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023]. $\tau_p = 7$ ms is a fixed nodal delay per hop representing synaptic transmission plus relay latency, consistent with the population-level excitatory/inhibitory synaptic time constants (5.8–7.3 ms) estimated directly from CCEP modelling [@lemarechal_brain_2022]. $\epsilon_\tau \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\tau)$, with $\sigma_\tau = 1$ ms, is a per-dipole jitter term modelling uncertainty in propagation timing, accumulated once per hop along the shortest path (i.e. scaling with $\sqrt{h_j}$ rather than a single flat perturbation of the total path delay). <!-- supp fig (propagation video)-->

**Noise model.** Pink noise was added at the source level to model background neural activity, and independent white noise was added at the sensor level to model measurement noise. Sensor-level noise comprised a small fixed instrument/electrode-noise floor (2.0 µV RMS) plus a source-space contribution solved to bring the total delivered sensor-level baseline noise to a target of 15.0 µV RMS — the literature midpoint of the commonly-cited ~10–20 µV RMS scalp EEG background noise range [@nunez_electric_2006]. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calibrated to a fixed single-trial target of 5 (peak amplitude relative to baseline standard deviation) by scaling the source activity prior to sensor projection: this sits above the ~2.0–3.2 linear-ratio range reported for single-trial interictal spikes [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024] <!-- Is gonsisko reporting peak to baseline? -->, chosen as a practical compromise to keep delivered spikes comfortably above the simulator's own noise floor while remaining much closer to the single-trial literature range than a post-averaging-scale target would be. All parameters are summarised in @tbl-sim-params.

Each simulation was repeated 8 times per source region. The number of regions and repetitions were set via a power analysis <!-- supp fig (power analysis, simf --> targeting adequate power for the region-paired method comparisons reported throughout the Results (see supplementary) — i.e., ensuring that the relative ranking of reconstruction methods is robust across a spatially-diverse sample of source regions rather than reflecting any single one (the main effect of method alone was already saturated at power ≈ 1.0 across every tested design).

### Clinical Dataset A — Resection Cohort

To validate electroencephalographic source imaging clinically, we used the dataset of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025, comprising 44 patients with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy who underwent resective surgery. Surgical outcome was assessed at 12 months post-operatively and graded on the ILAE scale (1 = seizure-free, 2–6 = increasing degrees of persistent seizures) [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025]. We restricted analysis to patients with a seizure-free outcome (ILAE 1), yielding 28 patients: for patients with residual seizures, the resection may not have fully encompassed the true epileptogenic zone, making the resected volume an unreliable ground truth for localization accuracy in that group. Resection masks were obtained as described in Section 2.5.1. Two further patients were excluded from the seizure-free subset: one had no genuine resection cavity for any candidate mask to capture, and the other was missing usable EEG channel locations for coregistration — yielding a final cohort of 26 patients. Each patient's data consisted of a pre-operative T1-weighted MRI and a pre-operative interictal EEG recording, as well as a post-operative T1-weighted MRI. The dataset provides 257-channel high-density EEG (HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net); cheek electrodes were excluded, yielding the 204-channel montage used throughout this study. Interictal epileptic discharges had been visually identified by clinical experts among the dataset's authors and were time-locked averaged at their peak.

Individual diffusion MRI was not available for this cohort, so the structural connectome was derived from the population probabilistic tractography atlas (Section 2.3.3) rather than subject-specific tractography.

## Signal Preprocessing


### EEG/iEEG Processing

**Studies 1 and 3 (Simulation and Simultaneous EEG/iEEG).** EEG data were available as epochs time-locked to the interictal spike peak — the known peak of the simulated source event in Study 1, and the peak of the simultaneously recorded intracranial (iEEG) signal in Study 3, rather than a peak independently detected on the scalp EEG itself. A Common Average Reference (CAR) was applied, consistent with standard practice for source reconstruction [@bertrand_theoretical_1985]. Baseline correction was performed using the pre-spike period, and an empirical noise covariance matrix was estimated from the same baseline window for subsequent data whitening. Epochs were then averaged to obtain the evoked response: exactly 20 spike epochs per simulated run in Study 1 (Section 2.1.1), and a variable number of clinically marked interictal spikes per subject in Study 3 (130–265 across the four subjects). For the Study 3 channel-comparison analysis (Section 2.6.3), the analysis window around each spike was defined by thresholding the global field power (GFP) of the evoked response: the continuous interval around the peak over which GFP stays above 3 standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline, rather than the fixed handful of samples around the peak used by @grova_intracranial_2016.

**Study 2 (Clinical Dataset A — resection cohort).** EEG data were provided as pre-averaged interictal discharge waveforms; individual epochs were not available. Preprocessing by the data providers included bandpass filtering (high-pass: 0.3–1 Hz; low-pass: 30–100 Hz, with filter settings varying across patients due to the longitudinal nature of the dataset), downsampling to 250 Hz, and interpolation of noisy channels from neighbouring electrodes using 3D splines. Since individual epochs were unavailable, noise covariance estimation and data whitening were not performed. A Common Average Reference was applied. A subset of subjects presented residual 50 Hz line noise and required an additional notch filter. Baseline correction was applied to subjects whose recordings lacked it.

**iEEG (Study 3).** Intracranial recordings were available as epochs time-locked to the spike peak. Epochs were averaged directly to obtain the ground-truth intracranial evoked response; no further preprocessing was applied.

## Forward Modeling and Structural Priors

### Source Space

We modeled neural activity using a distributed dipole model with a cortical constraint. The source space was restricted to the cortical white matter surface, reconstructed from T1-weighted MRI data using FreeSurfer (v7.4.1). Approximately 7,600 dipoles (oct6 icosahedral subdivision, after excluding medial-wall and non-cortical vertices) were uniformly distributed across this surface using MNE-Python (v1.9.0; @gramfort_meg_2013), at an average inter-dipole spacing of approximately 3.3 mm, with dipole orientations fixed normal to the cortical manifold — a constraint widely adopted in distributed source imaging because the dominant contributors to the EEG signal, pyramidal neurons, have net dipole moments oriented normal to the cortical surface [@dale_improved_1993].

### Volume Conduction Model

The forward problem involves calculating the electrical potential at the sensor locations generated by unitary dipole activity within the source space. To model the volume conduction between the sources and sensors, we employed a Boundary Element Model (BEM) [@hamalainen_realistic_1989]. A standard BEM represents the interfaces between major head tissues—specifically the inner skull, outer skull, and outer skin—assuming homogeneous and isotropic electrical conductivity within each compartment. We used the MNE-Python default conductivity values of 0.3 S/m for the brain and scalp, and 0.006 S/m for the skull. While MNE-Python typically relies on FreeSurfer's watershed algorithm for surface extraction, this approach often yields sub-optimal geometries for BEM. To improve the accuracy of the head model, we implemented a custom pipeline: brain tissues were segmented into three compartments (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). Each compartment mask was smoothed via morphological closing and fitted with a deformable grade-5 icosahedral template. The three surfaces were fitted sequentially — inner skull first, then outer skull, then scalp — with each surface constrained to lie outside the previous one, ensuring non-intersecting layers (see BEM improvement in supplementary) <!-- supp fig (BEM models)-->.

Since the EEG sensors were pre-co-registered to the T1-weighted MRI, they were intrinsically aligned with the resulting head model. The final forward solution (the gain matrix) was computed using MNE-Python. This forward solution was used across all three studies.

For Study 1 only, a second forward solution was computed for source reconstruction, with the skull conductivity increased to 0.012 S/m while keeping brain and scalp conductivities unchanged at 0.3 S/m. This deliberate mismatch avoids the inverse crime [@wirgin_inverse_2004] — the circularity that arises when the same head model is used for both generating and inverting simulated data, which artificially inflates reconstruction accuracy. A similar strategy — perturbing skull conductivity between the forward and inverse models to avoid this circularity — has been used elsewhere to probe the sensitivity of EEG source analysis to head-model mismatch [@vorwerk_skull_2014]. The two forward models differ by approximately 10% (see supplementary) <!-- supp fig (Head model differences)-->.

### Connectivity Matrices

In this work, the brain is modeled as a graph (or connectome) where nodes represent localized brain regions - specifically dipoles in our source space - and edges represent the structural scaffolding between them. For the Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) source reconstruction method and its weighted version (wCSET), we utilize a structural connectome, where edges represent physical anatomical links.

**Empirical connectomes**

We incorporate two distinct types of structural links:
1. Long-range connections: These represent white matter tracts (axonal bundles) estimated via diffusion MRI (dMRI) tractography.
2. Short-range connections: To account for local gray matter connectivity not captured by standard tractography, we connect each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors on the cortical manifold, subject to two constraints: a maximum geodesic distance of 15 mm, and a maximum of 8 such neighbors per dipole.

To ensure physical consistency, edges are weighted by distance (in mm): fiber length for long-range tracts and geodesic distance for local connections.

**Connectome surrogates**

In clinical settings where diffusion data may be unavailable, we evaluate three connectome surrogates validated through our simulation framework (see Section 3.1). Two of these are also tested in a binarized form (edge presence only, discarding distance weights) to separate the contribution of connectome topology from that of edge-weight fidelity — the Beltrami-operator surrogate has no such counterpart (see below) — five surrogate variants in total:
- Atlas surrogate: Long-range tracts are extrapolated from the MultiConn atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], built from a reference population of 66 subjects. We parcellate the subject's brain according to the atlas and identify region pairs connected by a tract present across all 66 subjects in the reference population. Instead of connecting every dipole pair between two such atlas-connected regions, only a fraction of the possible dipole-to-dipole edges is instantiated, at a sparsity level (14%) that we determined by matching the edge density of the single subject in our sample for whom an empirical structural connectome was available. Gray matter connections are then added as described above.
- Local surrogate: This model relies solely on gray matter connectivity derived from the brain mesh, with nodes additionally connected across hemispheres to their homotopic (mirror-symmetric) partner to keep the resulting graph connected <!-- CLAUDE: Only regions that are very close in euclidean space are connected to their homotopic partner. It the text it seems like all homotopic regions are connected. Please correct that. -->. While distinct from the Beltrami-operator geometry below, this surrogate tests the hypothesis that local brain geometry alone can capture significant brain-function coupling without explicit long-range information.
- Beltrami-operator surrogate: Eigenmodes are computed directly from the Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to the cortical mesh of each hemisphere, using the `lapy` Python library for the underlying finite-element stiffness/mass matrix assembly, without ever constructing an explicit dipole-to-dipole connectome. This mesh is the triangulation of the source space itself, in dipole space (Section 2.3.1) — the decimated, cortex-only surface used for the dipoles — rather than the dense FreeSurfer surface typically used for this computation [@pang_geometric_2023].<!-- Mention that we are doing the same thing as in the gbf paper. --> This is the purest geometry-only control: unlike the Local surrogate above, it does not threshold or weight a graph of geodesic distances at all, so there is no meaningful binarized counterpart to test.

**Connectome perturbation**
 
In the simulation, one has access to the exact connectome used to generate the data; in reality, one never has this exact knowledge. To evaluate robustness to this mismatch, we implemented a procedure to perturb the connectome before applying source reconstruction (see Section 3.1.2): a degree-preserving double-edge swap, in which two existing edges are picked at random and their endpoints re-paired to form two new edges, so that each node's total number of connections is left unchanged.

Perturbation severity is expressed as a percentage of the connectome's total edge count, ranging from 0% (the original, unperturbed connectome) to 100%, at which point as good as none of the original edges remain.

**Graph Fourier Transform**
The connectome edges described above are weighted by the element-wise inverse of their distances (fiber length for long-range tracts, geodesic distance for short-range links), so that spatially closer, more direct structural connections receive proportionally larger weight than distant ones — the natural convention for a graph meant to capture how strongly two dipoles are structurally coupled, since raw distance alone would otherwise assign the largest values to the weakest, most indirect links. These inverse-distance weights populate the connectome's adjacency matrix A, from which we compute the graph Laplacian L = D − A (where D is the degree matrix) — the representation that allows us to apply the tools of Graph Signal Processing (GSP) to neural data [@shuman_emerging_2013; @ortega_graph_2018].

Just as the classical Fourier Transform decomposes a time-series into sine and cosine waves, the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) decomposes brain activity into a set of graph harmonics. These harmonics are the eigenvectors $u_k$ of the Graph Laplacian, obtained via the eigendecomposition: 
$$
\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top
$$

where $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ contains the eigenvalues (graph frequencies) and $\mathbf{U} = [u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_N]$ forms the orthonormal eigenbasis.


## Source Reconstruction Framework

For every study, we used MNE-Python's widely used methods wMNE [@dale_improved_1993], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000] and sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002] (see Section 2.4.1), and compare these to three connectivity-informed methods CSET, wCSET and GBF (see Section 2.4.2). All methods used data whitening based on an empirically estimated noise covariance matrix — a standard preprocessing step in linear M/EEG source reconstruction that decorrelates and normalizes sensor noise before inversion [@dale_dynamic_2000; @knosche_eegmeg_2022] — with one exception: for the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A), the data were provided as pre-averaged discharges with no accompanying baseline epochs, so no empirical noise covariance could be computed, and an ad-hoc (identity-like) covariance was used instead, i.e. no whitening.

### Standard Inverse Solutions

In the M/EEG inverse problem, we aim to estimate underlying dipole activities $\mathbf s\in \mathbb R^n$ from observed sensor measurements $\mathbf y \in \mathbb R^m$. This relationship is defined by the forward model:

$$
\mathbf y = \mathbf L \mathbf s + \epsilon
$$

where $\mathbf L$ is the lead-field matrix and $\epsilon$ represents additive noise. Because the number of dipoles greatly exceeds the number of sensors ($n\gg m$), the problem is ill-posed and lacks a unique solution without further constraints.

From a Bayesian perspective, $\mathbf s$ is treated as a random variable with a prior distribution $P(\mathbf s)$ [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Assuming a Gaussian prior $\mathbf s \sim \mathcal N(0, \Sigma_{\mathbf s})$, reconstruction becomes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation, leading to the optimization problem:
$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\underbrace{\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2}_{\text{Data Fidelity}} + \lambda\underbrace{\lVert \mathbf C \mathbf s\rVert_p^p}_{\text{Regularization}} \tag{1}
$$

Here, $\lambda$ is the regularization parameter balancing data fit with prior assumptions. The matrix $\mathbf C$ acts as a weighting matrix derived from the prior covariance, such that $\mathbf C^T\mathbf C = \mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1}$. In practice, the true source covariance $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ is unknown and replaced with the identity matrix — the assumption of independent, equal-variance sources that gives wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA their "independent-source" label throughout this work.

wMNE additionaly ajusts source variances generating the depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ applied to counteract the bias of $l_2$-regularized solutions toward superficial dipoles:

$$
\mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1} = \mathbf W_d, \qquad \text{where} \quad W_{d,ii} = \lVert \mathbf L_{:i}\rVert^{-\kappa}
$$

For wMNE, the depth-weighting exponent was set to $\kappa=0.8$, the MEG-optimized value reported by @lin_assessing_2006 (who found a higher optimal range, 2.0–5.0, for EEG specifically). sLORETA and dSPM apply an additional post-hoc standardization on top of the minimum-norm estimate, and were run without additional depth weighting, since this noise-normalization step already compensates for depth bias on its own.

While it is widely accepted that source activity is heavily interdependent [@bressler_large-scale_2010], these independent-source assumptions are typically chosen because estimating source co-dependence has remained computationally or theoretically elusive. The methods introduced next address this gap directly, by embedding structural connectivity into the source-covariance prior itself.

### Connectivity-Informed Inverse Solution

This section describes the three connectivity-informed inverse solutions compared throughout this work, introduced in order: CSET [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024], the connectome-spectrum $l_1$ sparsity prior our approach builds on; weighted CSET (wCSET), this work's central methodological contribution, which replaces CSET's $l_1$ prior with a smooth, harmonic-weighted $l_2$ prior over the connectome spectrum; and GBF [@wang_geometry_2026], a geometry-based method that shares wCSET's smooth $l_2$ formulation but operates on the eigenbasis of cortical geometry rather than the connectome.

**Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography**

Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024] addresses the independence limitation, by operating in a component-based space. Instead of solving for activity in the brain's physical space, CSET projects the activity onto the eigenmodes of the connectome ($\mathbf U$). This transforms the problem into the "connectome spectrum" space, where the prior can be more effectively described. As with wMNE, CSET and wCSET first counteract the bias toward superficial dipoles with the same depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ (defined above), applied directly to the lead field prior to projection onto the eigenbasis; unlike wMNE's literature-standard $\kappa=0.8$, CSET and wCSET use $\kappa=0.2$, tuned against reconstruction accuracy in the simulation study (Section 3.1).

Given that the connectome spectrum is known to be compact, CSET enforces sparsity by applying an $l_1$​-norm to the regularizer. Let $\mathbf {\hat s}$ represent the spectrum of $\mathbf s$ (where $\mathbf s = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}$). Equation (1) is then modified to: 
$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_1 \tag{2}
$$

The physical brain activity is then recovered via $\mathbf s^* = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf{\hat s}^*$.

**weighted CSET**

While basic CSET enforces sparsity, it does not necessarily distinguish between signal and noise in a physiologically informed way. We address this with weighted CSET (wCSET), which replaces CSET's $l_1$ sparsity prior with a smooth, weighted $l_2$ prior over the connectome spectrum. Harmonic weights follow an exponential low-pass filter on graph frequency, $W_{h,ii} = \exp(-\beta\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is harmonic $i$'s eigenvalue and $\beta$ controls the filter's decay rate, tuned against this connectome's own reconstruction accuracy. This form remains compact since the signal is compressed in the low frequencies and is motivated by the structure–function coupling literature: functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, i.e. a small number of low-frequency structural harmonics dominate functional coupling [@abdelnour_functional_2018]. Equation (2) thus becomes:

$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf W_h\mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 \tag{3}
$$

where $\mathbf W_h$ is the diagonal matrix of harmonic weights above. Unlike CSET's $l_1$ sparsity prior, which selects a small number of active harmonics, wCSET's $l_2$ prior smoothly downweights high-frequency harmonics while leaving the low-frequency end of the spectrum comparatively unpenalized. The physical brain activity is again recovered via $\mathbf s^* = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf{\hat s}^*$.

Neither CSET nor wCSET is tied to a particular way of building the connectome that defines $\mathbf U$. What the framework requires is a structural graph whose edges reflect the strength of information flow between dipoles; how that graph is estimated (dMRI tractography, as used here, or an alternative that forgoes an explicit graph altogether, such as the Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to the cortical mesh, Section 2.3.3) and how its edges are weighted (inverse geodesic/fiber distance, as used here, but equally fiber count or raw fiber length) are choices external to the formalism itself. The specific connectome construction adopted in this work (Section 2.3.3) is one principled instantiation, motivated by the structure–function coupling literature [@abdelnour_functional_2018].

**Geometric Basis Functions**

As a further reference method, we reconfigure wCSET (Eq. 3) to reproduce Wang et al. (2026)'s Geometric Basis Functions (GBF) [@wang_geometry_2026] as closely as our framework allows, rather than reimplementing their exact pipeline — mesh resolution and regularization differ. Three changes distinguish this GBF-like variant from the connectome-based wCSET above: (i) the connectome eigenbasis $\mathbf U$ is replaced by the eigenvectors of the Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to the cortical mesh (Section 2.3.3), so the spectral decomposition reflects cortical geometry rather than white-matter connectivity; (ii) no depth weighting is applied ($\mathbf W_d = \mathbf I$), matching GBF's original formulation, which includes no depth term; and (iii) wCSET's smooth exponential harmonic weights (Eq. 3) are replaced by a log-form weighting adapted from GBF's own logarithmic spectral prior, $W_{h,ii} = \sqrt{-\log(\mu_i/\mu_S)}$ for the $S$ lowest-frequency Beltrami eigenmodes and $W_{h,ii}=0$ beyond, where $\mu_i$ denotes the Laplace-Beltrami operator's eigenvalues (as opposed to the connectome graph Laplacian's $\lambda_i$ used in Eq. 3). This weighting differs from wCSET's in two independent ways: the truncation is hard rather than smoothly decaying, and its log-form shape was selected by Wang et al. on empirical grounds, unlike wCSET's exponential form, which follows directly from the structure–function coupling rationale of Eq. 3 [@abdelnour_functional_2018]. We set $S=150$, tuned against reconstruction accuracy in the simulation study (Section 3.1), rather than the $S=300$ used in the original GBF publication: Wang et al. tune a scale parameter $\beta$ for their log-form weighting, but our pipeline trace-renormalizes the inverse kernel before the ridge solve (standard practice), which renders $\beta$ a pure rescale with no effect on the reconstruction. Rather than leave this comparator's one nominally free parameter untuned, we instead tuned the parameter that actually shapes the weighting under our normalization, the cutoff $S$: a sweep against simulated ground truth showed $S=150$ roughly halving peak-localization error relative to $S=300$ (6.1 vs. 14.7 mm) while matching or exceeding it on average precision. This geometry-only comparator, in the spirit of GBF and related cortical-geometry approaches [@pang_geometric_2023; @wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026] (Section 1), is tested as a connectome surrogate in the simulation study (Section 3.1.4), and included as a full fourth reference method in the two clinical studies (Sections 3.2, 3.3).

## Clinical Ground Truth Definition

In contrast to the simulated framework, we usually do not have the exact brain activity maps to evaluate source reconstruction methods. We therefore use proxies which allow us to test specific aspects of the method. In the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A; Section 2.1.2), we use the fact that patients underwent surgery, had a brain section removed, and were symptom-free of epilepsy after the surgery. We use the resected area as ground truth to measure the source localization error. We therefore need to segment the resected area (see Section 2.5.1). In the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B; Section 2.1.3), we have the recordings of electric potential inside the brain, but only in a few areas. For that, we need to estimate the underlying potential generated by our reconstructed maps (which show dipole currents) at the same locations as the intracranial channels. We use for that a simplified version of the forward problem (see Section 2.5.2).

### Resected Area Segmentation

This section applies to the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A; Section 2.1.2). Resection masks were generated using RAMPS [@simpson_automated_2025], an automated segmentation-and-registration pipeline that estimates the resected volume directly from a subject's pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI. RAMPS additionally requires the hemisphere of the resection and the resected lobe (temporal, frontal, parietal, occipital, or a combination thereof) as input: the lobe was unambiguous from the clinical record for temporal resections, and was determined by visual comparison of the pre- and post-operative images for extratemporal resections. Resulting masks underwent visual quality review by overlaying the pre-operative T1w, post-operative T1w, and resection mask, and were replaced with a manually-segmented mask for a minority of patients whose automated mask was unusable on this review or for whom RAMPS could not be run; subjects whose mask remained missing, incomplete, or clearly incorrect after this process were excluded (Section 2.1.2).

### Source-to-iEEG Projection

This section applies to the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B; Section 2.1.3). Following source reconstruction, the estimated cortical activity was projected onto the coordinates of the intracranial electrodes to generate "virtual" iEEG potentials. This projection followed the methodology of Grova et al. (2016) [@grova_intracranial_2016]. Given that this step assumes the sources and sensors reside within the same compartment, we modeled this as an infinite homogeneous conduction problem. The potential $\Phi$ at a location $r$ is estimated from the brain activity as:
$$
\Phi(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3}
$$

Following the adjustments proposed by Cosandier-Rimélé et al. (2007) [@cosandier-rimele_physiologically_2007], the brain tissue conductivity (σ) was set to 0.25 S/m (modified from the standard 0.33 S/m) to compensate for the simplifications inherent in the homogeneous model. Assuming an iEEG-MRI coregistration accuracy of 3 mm, we use the same model adjustement to prevent instabilities of the model caused by too close measurements: 

$$
\begin{align}\Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r>r_0 = 3 \text{ mm} \\ \Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r\le r_0 = 3 \text{ mm}\end{align}
$$

## Performance Evaluation Metrics

### Map to map comparison

To evaluate each method we compute the (signed) Pearson spatial correlation between the reconstructed and ground-truth activity maps at each time point:
$$
\mathcal{C}(t) = \frac{\sum_i \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{true}}(i) \cdot \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{est}}(i)}{\sigma_{\text{true}}(t) \cdot \sigma_{\text{est}}(t)}
$$

where $\mathbf s^t_{x}(i)$ is the activity at dipole $i$ and time $t$, and $\sigma_{x}(t)$ is the standard deviation of map $x$ at time $t$.

### Localization Accuracy

To evaluate localization accuracy, the source onset of the interictal spikes was defined relative to the rising phase of the discharge: this time point is a pragmatic compromise between a low probability that the source has already started propagating (favoring the discharge's onset) and an adequate signal-to-noise ratio (favoring the discharge's peak, by which point the source has typically already spread). For both the resection cohort and the simulation dataset, we used 25% of the rising phase (quarter rising phase, qrp), earlier than the 50% (half rising phase) convention of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020. The Euclidean distance was then calculated between the estimated source location and the target mask — the true seed region for the simulation dataset, or the resection volume for the resection cohort. Rather than working around voxel-grid discretization by averaging distances to several nearest voxels, we follow @carboni_linear_2022 and @wang_geometry_2026 and report the minimum Euclidean distance from the location of maximal source activity to the mask boundary, taken as 0 mm whenever that location already lies inside the mask.

### Network Concentration Index

Peak-vertex localization accuracy (above) only tests whether the single most active location falls near the resection. Epilepsy is increasingly understood as a network disorder, in which interictal discharges may arise from a distributed set of regions only partially captured by the resected tissue [@spencer_neural_2002; @kramer_epilepsy_2012]; testing whether reconstructed activity concentrates on the resected zone as a whole, not just at its single peak, offers a complementary view of localization. We define the Network Concentration Index (NCI): cortical vertices are ranked by absolute source activity magnitude and progressively marked active from the highest-ranked down, until a spatially contiguous cluster of area ≥ 600 mm² — the literature-established minimum synchronously active cortex needed to produce a scalp-visible interictal discharge [@grova_evaluation_2006] — first overlaps the resection. NCI is the fraction of total cortical surface area that had to be marked active for this to occur, expressed as a percentage; lower values indicate that the reconstructed network's most active regions converge more tightly onto the resected zone. As with Localization Accuracy, NCI is computed at the quarter and full rising phase for the resection cohort, using the resected volume as ground truth (Section 2.5.1). We additionally calibrate NCI against a chance level: the cortical area fraction a purely random, spatially unstructured activity map needs before any cluster — regardless of whether it overlaps the resection — reaches the 600 mm² floor, isolating the contribution of the size threshold itself from genuine localization performance.

### Channel comparison

To evaluate the accuracy of the spatial reconstruction, the projected virtual iEEG activity (Section 2.5.2) was compared against the recorded ground-truth iEEG using the (polarity-invariant) Pearson correlation between estimated and ground-truth channel activity, computed in two modes: spatially (across channels, at each timepoint) and temporally (across time, for each channel). Polarity invariance is obtained by taking the absolute value of the raw correlation ($|r|$) rather than the signed value, since an overall sign flip is an arbitrary consequence of the virtual-electrode reference convention rather than a meaningful failure mode.

For each competing method, we additionally compute a win-rate against wCSET — the fraction of channels (or time points) on which wCSET's estimate is closer to ground truth than the competitor's — summarizing pairwise performance relative to our proposed method, rather than a full all-against-all comparison across every method pair.

To test the impact of neglecting source dependences we created a simulation that is constrained by the structural connectivity. This allows us to have simulated EEG recordings with complex ground truth activity. @fig-flagship-example (a) shows an example of an EEG recording with the key events happening. We have the peak phase, where the EEG signal is highest. At that phase, similar to what is suggested in the literature, the source has already started to propagate. Generally, it is advised to reconstruct around 50% of the rising phase (or even before if the signal to noise permits it) to properly locate the source [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022]; here, the simulation's controlled SNR permits reconstructing earlier, at 25% of the rising phase (quarter rising phase, qrp). We consider as the source propagation phase everything happening after the quarter rising phase until the signal is back to noise level. We then applied source reconstruction using the five methods described in Section 2.4 (wMNE, sLORETA, dSPM, and the connectivity-informed CSET and wCSET), and compared the accuracy of source localization across methods at the quarter rising phase (25% of the rising phase; @fig-localization-qrp). At single-trial SNR = 5, wCSET's localization error was significantly higher than CSET's and dSPM's, and significantly lower than sLORETA's and wMNE's (Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, paired by region, FDR-corrected: CSET p < 0\.001, r = 0\.23; dSPM p < 0\.001, r = 0\.22; sLORETA p < 0\.0001, r = \-0\.46; wMNE p < 0\.0001, r = \-0\.94).

We also computed the spatial correlation time point by time point between the simulated ground truth and the reconstructions for all our source reconstruction methods, letting us evaluate not only which method best captures the source's extent at the quarter rising phase, but also which best reconstructs its propagation at the peak phase. For each region, we averaged spatial correlation across its repeated simulations, then plotted the median of these per-region averages — together with their interquartile range across regions — over time in @fig-correlation-time. Cluster-based permutation testing (region-paired, FDR-corrected across competitors) confirmed this pattern: wCSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth was significantly higher than every competitor's across nearly the entire displayed window, spanning both the quarter rising phase and the peak (approximately \-12 to 116 ms for sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE, and \-12 to 108 ms for CSET; all p_corrected < 0\.001). Effect sizes were markedly larger against the three standard methods (Cohen's dz = 4\.26 sLORETA, 3\.84 dSPM, 5\.98 wMNE) than against CSET (dz = 2\.10), and the correlation gap between the two connectivity-informed methods (wCSET, CSET) and the three standard methods was itself widest around the peak phase (t ≈ 16 ms).

:::{#2dd22c28 .cell .markdown}
In the simulation, the true connectome is known; in practice it never is exactly. To test what happens when the wrong connectome is used, we systematically permuted the true connectome before reconstruction (Section 2.3.3) and re-evaluated localization error (@fig-degradation-localization) and spatial correlation (@fig-degradation-correlation) for CSET and wCSET, this time benchmarked directly against sLORETA rather than against each other: sLORETA is connectome-agnostic, so its performance cannot be affected by connectome corruption, making it a natural floor — the degradation level at which a connectivity-informed method becomes significantly worse than sLORETA is the point past which using the (corrupted) connectome is actively counterproductive, rather than merely less helpful. dSPM remains connectome-agnostic too and is shown only as a flat, untested reference line.

wCSET's localization error remained essentially flat under permutation up to 60% (4\.4–9\.1 mm), only climbing noticeably beyond that point (11\.4 mm at 70%, 23\.1 mm at 100%). Benchmarked against sLORETA (region-paired cluster-permutation), wCSET was significantly *more* accurate across low-to-moderate degradation (0–70%, p_corrected < 0\.001, Cohen's dz = \-0\.89), and never became significantly worse than sLORETA at any degradation level tested, including full (100%) permutation. CSET showed the same early advantage over a comparable range (0–60%, p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = \-0\.69), but unlike wCSET this advantage reversed: CSET became significantly worse than sLORETA from 80% onward (p_corrected = 0\.014, dz = 0\.57) — a degradation level at which wCSET's own localization error never reached a significant deficit, even under full connectome permutation.
:::

Simulation offers a controlled testbed, but real clinical data will always differ. To verify that connectivity-informed source localization remains competitive with standard clinical methods in practice — rather than trading focal precision for network sensitivity — we evaluated localization accuracy against the resected epileptogenic zone in seizure-free patients (ILAE 1, n=26).

Alongside wMNE, sLORETA, and dSPM, we also compared against a Beltrami-eigenbasis variant of wCSET — the same Laplace-Beltrami mesh eigenmodes used as a connectome surrogate in Section 3.1.4, here run as a full 6th competitor method, in the spirit of the cortical-geometry approache of @wang_geometry_2026 (Section 1).

Peak-to-resection distance behaved similarly across most methods (@fig-resection-localization): wCSET's median distance (9\.6 mm) was descriptively the lowest, with Beltrami's the closest runner-up (17\.2 mm), ahead of sLORETA (18\.1 mm), CSET (18\.8 mm), and dSPM (25\.5 mm), with wMNE a clear outlier (31\.1 mm). Of the five paired comparisons against wCSET, only wMNE reached significance after FDR correction (Wilcoxon signed-rank, subject-paired: p_corrected = 0\.005, r = \-0\.54); CSET (p_corrected = 0\.077, r = \-0\.44), sLORETA (p_corrected = 0\.077, r = \-0\.48), dSPM (p_corrected = 0\.077, r = \-0\.46), and Beltrami (p_corrected = 0\.493, r = 0\.12) were not significantly different from wCSET.

The Network Concentration Index (NCI) told a different story: wCSET required markedly less of the cortex to be marked active before a cluster first touched the resection (median 1\.3% vs. 2\.0–7\.7% for the other methods) — and, contrary to our initial impression of a small effect, this difference was significant for every comparison (Wilcoxon signed-rank, subject-paired, FDR-corrected: CSET p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.92; dSPM p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.92; sLORETA p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.92; wMNE p_corrected < 0\.001, r = \-0\.77; Beltrami p_corrected = 0\.009, r = \-0\.46), all well below the 31\.6% chance level. The effect was large for CSET, sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE (|r| = 0\.77–0\.92) but visibly smaller for Beltrami (r = \-0\.46), whose median (2\.0%) came closest to wCSET's on this metric too. This indicates that the top-ranked source activity is substantially more concentrated on the true epileptogenic zone for wCSET than for any comparator method — most consistently so against CSET, sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE, and to a lesser degree against the geometry-only Beltrami variant — even though overall peak localization accuracy remains statistically comparable across methods (wMNE excepted).

## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG)

### Spatial and Temporal Correlation Analysis

Source localization was inconclusive for connectivity-informed methods in Study II — comparable to, but not clearly better than, standard methods (Section 3.2.1). Because these methods are designed to capture distributed activity rather than a single focal source, we instead tested whether they better reproduce the overall pattern of activity, as the simulation results in Section 3.1 suggest they should.

Of the four subjects with usable simultaneous EEG/iEEG data (Section 2.1.3), two show a visible interictal spike on the scalp EEG; the remaining two have deep sources producing no visible spike on the EEG despite clear intracranial evidence of the same interictal discharge, and are reported in the supplementary material rather than the main text below (<!-- supp figure (sub-12/sub-50: wCSET - competitor paired differences, per channel/timepoint) -->). For each subject we compared wCSET against every competitor at the level of individual channels (temporal correlation: how well each channel's own time-course matches the true intracranial recording) and individual timepoints (spatial correlation: how well the pattern across channels matches at each instant), using a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (n_eff) in place of the raw channel/timepoint count, since neighbouring channels and timepoints from the same subject and spike are not independent observations.

# Discussion

## Simulation take home message

The simulation begins as a focal source and spreads across the brain, its amplitude decaying with the number of graph hops from the origin. Propagation can follow neighboring dipoles step by step, but it can also take shortcuts through long-range tracts, letting distant regions rise above the noise floor that pure nearest-neighbor spread could never reach — a mechanism absent from neural field models.

A neural mass model [@jansen_electroencephalogram_1995] would capture this more physiologically, but such models become unstable at high mass counts, since network size and coupling strength jointly determine whether the system stays in a stable dynamical regime [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015]. This is why other source-reconstruction studies typically cap the number of masses around 1,000, with dipoles spaced roughly 1 cm apart [@siu_structural_2026]. At that spacing, though, the forward model's own assumption — that each dipole's effective area is much smaller than its distance to the sensors — starts to break down [@nunez_multi-scale_2019].

Our patch-seeded, connectome-driven propagation model avoids this trade-off: it keeps the dipole model at high resolution (~7,600 dipoles, ~3.3 mm spacing) while staying simple enough to generate realistic EEG spikes. The source itself is a spatial patch, but the propagated pattern is not — it can reach non-adjacent regions directly via long-range tracts rather than only spreading outward through neighbors. We do not claim this simulation is more faithful to reality than neural mass or field models, only that it offers insight a simple patch simulation cannot, while remaining tractable at high dipole counts.

This design has a further consequence: the EEG signal's peak systematically lags the true onset of the source. The source's own amplitude is highest at the origin and decays as it spreads, but the scalp signal sums contributions from every active dipole at once — so it keeps rising as the pattern reaches more of the cortex, even as the origin itself fades. This cumulative summation is what pushes the scalp peak to arrive only once the source has already spread considerably, consistent with the broader clinical literature on interictal discharge propagation [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022]. It is precisely why the field favors an earlier point in the rising phase over the peak for localization: at that point the signal is already detectable, but activity remains close to the true onset, with only limited spread having occurred.

### Localization versus spread

Most simulation-based source-reconstruction studies focus on localization and report both location and spatial extent. At the quarter rising phase the source is still relatively focal, and methods like sLORETA and dSPM — designed to optimize localization rather than extent — should be at their best. wCSET's localization error at this phase differed significantly from every other method (Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, paired by region, FDR-corrected; Section 3.1.1), but not by the same margin in every case. Against CSET and dSPM it was modestly *less* accurate, with effect sizes small enough that the three methods localize the source about equally well at this early, focal phase. Its advantage over sLORETA was more substantial, and its advantage over wMNE was large — wMNE was a clear outlier, not just the weakest by a small margin. With 100 simulated regions behind each test, even small differences reach significance, so it is the effect sizes rather than the p-values that separate a meaningful gap (wMNE, and to a lesser extent sLORETA) from an essentially negligible one (CSET, dSPM).

We do not report extent using precision/recall-style metrics [@bradley_evaluation_2016], since thresholding reconstructed activity into a binary "active" mask requires an arbitrary cutoff. Spatial correlation with the ground truth serves as a proxy instead, and the higher correlation already visible for wCSET and CSET at the quarter rising phase hints at a genuine improvement in extent, consistent with reports from similar connectivity- and geometry-informed methods [@wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026]. This likely reflects the fact that connectivity matrices encode local, neighboring connections, which help define spatially coherent patches of activity.

Connectivity-informed reconstruction offers more than better extent, though: because it is constrained by the brain's actual connections, it also addresses the spread problem directly. Spatial correlation with the ground truth improves markedly for every method as the signal spreads toward the EEG peak — partly because SNR is also higher there, which is why even sLORETA's correlation rises over the same window. But the gain is far larger for wCSET and CSET, and the connectome-spectrum literature explains why: as activity spreads across the cortex, its representation becomes increasingly compact in the connectome-harmonic domain, tracking the signal's own power [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. A spreading source becomes progressively better described by a small number of graph harmonics — exactly the representation wCSET and CSET are built around — which is why their correlation gain outpaces the others as the peak approaches. What matters for comparing methods, then, is not that correlation rises for everyone, but the widening gap between connectivity-informed and connectivity-agnostic methods over that same window.

### Robustness to inaccuracies

We also tested robustness by repeating source reconstruction across a range of single-trial SNRs and connectome degradation levels, rather than the single SNR=5 used above (Section 3.1.2). On localization error, wMNE was again the outlier — already several times wCSET's error at the highest SNR tested, and significantly worse across the entire range — while wCSET, CSET, sLORETA, and dSPM behaved similarly to one another, staying low until around SNR=4–5 before climbing together. Spatial correlation was more informative: wCSET significantly outperformed all four competitors at both the quarter rising phase and the peak across nearly the whole SNR range, with effect sizes from moderate to very large, holding even at low SNR. (One caveat: SNR was calibrated on the single trial, before the 20-epoch averaging used for reconstruction, so it does not directly equal the SNR of the reconstructed evoked response; we did not separately test how averaging more or fewer epochs would interact with this.)

Connectome degradation told a more informative story. Under permutation, CSET's spatial correlation stayed comparatively flat through 60% degradation (Section 3.1.3), suggesting that the harmonics driving reconstruction accuracy might simply be the most robust ones, regardless of graph frequency. We first tried to encode this directly, weighting harmonics with a U-shaped profile based on @sipes_integrative_2024's finding that robustness to connectome perturbation follows the gap-spectrum (the difference between consecutive eigenvalues) — favoring both integrative (low-frequency) and segregative (high-frequency) harmonics over the intermediate, degenerate ones. In practice, though, retaining the high-frequency end of this U introduced visible reconstruction artifacts, likely because high-frequency harmonics are so sparse. We narrowed our focus to the low-frequency end alone instead, in line with the broader literature, and adopted an exponential decay over that range — the choice that became wCSET — which improved on CSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth.

Benchmarked against the connectome-agnostic sLORETA baseline, CSET's early advantage on both metrics reversed into a significant deficit by 80% permutation, while wCSET's advantage never reversed on either metric, even under full (100%) permutation — holding significant through 70–80% before becoming statistically indistinguishable from sLORETA thereafter. As degradation increased, wCSET and CSET converged toward each other and toward the sLORETA/dSPM baselines, as expected: a fully permuted connectome carries no genuine structural information, leaving both methods in the same position as the two that never used the connectome at all. This tolerance for substantial rewiring is encouraging given the well-documented tendency of tractography to produce more false-positive than true-positive white matter bundles [@maier-hein_challenge_2017], and it suggests that even fairly crude connectome surrogates should support reasonable reconstruction accuracy — a hypothesis we test directly next.

### Using surrogates

We tested three ways to build a connectome surrogate for when subject-specific dMRI is unavailable — extrapolating from a published atlas, relying purely on cortical geometry via our own local-connectivity rule, and the increasingly popular Laplace-Beltrami operator — each also tested in binarized (presence/absence) form to isolate the contribution of edge weights from topology. Somewhat surprisingly, wCSET's localization error was significantly *more* accurate using every surrogate than using the true connectome (Section 3.1.4). Effect sizes were only small to moderate, but consistent across all five surrogates — none stood out as meaningfully better than the rest.

Spatial correlation showed the same direction of effect, more strongly: every surrogate produced a significant improvement over the true connectome, growing from small at the quarter rising phase to substantial by the peak, most markedly for Beltrami. Even so, wCSET's correlation with any surrogate remained roughly 3–4× higher than dSPM's or sLORETA's own correlation using the *true* connectome. Binarized and weighted versions of the atlas and local surrogates performed almost identically, suggesting that topology, not precise edge weights, drives the benefit.
