This is why we carry the Beltrami-based GBF variant (Section 2.4.2) forward as a full reference method in the clinical studies that follow: if geometry alone can rival, or even edge out, a subject's true white-matter connectome in simulation, it deserves to be tested directly against real, clinically validated ground truth too.

### Limitations

These simulations let us probe source-reconstruction behavior under fully known ground truth, but they necessarily idealize several aspects of real recordings: known conductivities (aside from the deliberate forward-model mismatch, Section 2.3.2), a single representative subject, and propagation/noise models that, while physiologically motivated, remain simplified. Some of these assumptions may not hold in real brains — which is why the rest of this Discussion turns to clinical data, evaluating the same methods against ground truths that are not simulated: resection outcome and simultaneous intracranial recordings, each with its own different limitations.

## Epilepsy with Resected Ground Truth

This dataset lets us test source localization against a widely accepted clinical benchmark. The simulation already suggested that connectivity information brings little improvement in single-source localization accuracy relative to CSET specifically (Section 3.1.1), and this evaluation — using an approach similar to the prior literature — largely confirms that picture: peak-to-resection distance did not differ significantly between wCSET and CSET, sLORETA, dSPM, or Beltrami (included here as a further geometry-based comparator, per Section 3.1.4), whose median distance came closest to wCSET's of any competitor (Section 3.2.1). wMNE was the one clear exception, significantly less accurate than wCSET — echoing its role as the outlier in simulation too.

This evaluation has two notable limitations. First, we lack a precise delineation of the epileptogenic zone, only the coarser resected volume as a proxy. Second, localization accuracy here is considerably worse than in simulation: given the resection volume's typical size, a source localized as accurately as in simulation should fall inside it almost every time. Instead, clinical reconstructions show a more complicated picture: sLORETA's activity is diffuse and only partially overlaps the resection, with its single maximum falling outside it, while wCSET's reconstruction breaks into several discrete blobs, only some of which overlap the resected area. This may reflect an underestimate of physiological noise in our simulations, or that the clinical interictal discharge has already spread considerably by the 50% rising phase — in wCSET's case, into a genuinely multi-focal pattern rather than a single displaced peak.

This mismatch motivated a complementary metric — the smallest fraction of cortex that must be marked active before a cluster first touches the resection (the Network Concentration Index, Section 2.6.3) — since reconstructions at the 50% rising phase already show multiple discrete regions of activity, whether from genuine spread or because the spike never depended on a single region. Here the picture sharpened considerably: wCSET required significantly less cortex than every other method, including Beltrami, to reach the resection zone — a large effect against the four connectome-agnostic and CSET comparators, and a smaller but still significant one against Beltrami, whose reconstructions again came closest to wCSET's. All methods nonetheless reached the resection zone well before chance level: the true focus is reconstructed correctly by every method, but missed by metrics that only consider the single peak vertex. wCSET's advantage lies in how much less of the reconstructed activity outside that peak is superfluous.

This is consistent with genuine spread, but also with the now well-established view that epilepsy is a network phenomenon rather than a single-generator disease [@spencer_neural_2002; @kramer_epilepsy_2012]: several regions might jointly sustain a positive-feedback loop that generates the interictal discharge, so that removing any single node of that loop could relieve symptoms without resecting the point of maximal reconstructed activity. Delineating such networks directly is beyond the scope of the present work, but this cluster-based view could in principle support it.

## Epilepsy with Intracranial Electrodes

Intracranial electrodes measure true electrical activity inside the brain, but cover only a small fraction of it and record potential rather than dipole current directly. Comparing them to source reconstructions therefore requires projecting reconstructed sources onto the intracranial channel locations — an additional, error-prone step. We adopted Grova's projection approach (Section 2.5.2) but defined our own comparison metrics. Grova's original method focuses mainly on the spike peak, considering at most the five time points around it (about 3.3 ms, at their reported 1200 Hz sampling rate). To test whether wCSET improves reconstruction during the spike's spread as well, as our simulations predict, we extended this to the full GFP-threshold spike window (Section 2.2.1) — the continuous interval around the peak where global field power stays above a fixed multiple of the pre-spike baseline — rather than a fixed five-sample neighborhood. We also excluded Grova's measure of spurious activity, since it assumes activity elsewhere in the brain is necessarily an artifact, at odds with the premise that spike-related activity can genuinely be distributed.

Two of the four subjects have deep sources: despite clear evidence of the spike intracranially, no corresponding spike is visible on the scalp EEG. Unsurprisingly, no method reconstructs the intracranial channels well in these two subjects — a limitation also reported in Grova's own work. The two subjects with a visible EEG spike responded very differently (Section 3.3.1).

Subject 1 showed wCSET's clearest advantage: significantly higher spatial correlation with the true intracranial recording than sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET, winning a majority of individual timepoints against each — though the temporal-correlation advantage was more modest, reaching significance only against wMNE. Subject 2 showed no comparable advantage: the only significant difference against these four methods was a temporal edge over CSET, with wCSET otherwise statistically indistinguishable from sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE.

Against the Beltrami-based GBF variant carried over from Section 3.1.4, however, the picture reversed in both subjects: wCSET's spatial correlation was significantly *lower* than Beltrami's in subject 1, and its temporal correlation significantly lower in subject 2 — smaller effects than wCSET's advantages over the other four methods, but a reversal nonetheless. Taken together with the surrogate results in Section 3.1.4, this is, to our knowledge, the first evidence from real, non-simulated brain activity that a purely geometric account of source reconstruction can match or exceed a connectome-informed one — exactly the kind of test our simulation, built around one particular true connectome, could never offer on its own.

Two caveats apply. Within each subject, we corrected the effective sample size for autocorrelation across channels/timepoints rather than treating them as independent observations, but this does not address the separate limitation that only four subjects are available in total, which precludes any statistical test across independent subjects. We also did not adopt Grova's patch-wise reconstruction approach; in exchange, our data have a genuine advantage over Grova's, since scalp EEG and intracranial recordings were acquired simultaneously rather than separately, as in Grova's work, where the two modalities could not be recorded together for MEG-specific reasons.

A further limitation is the framework's reliance on a cortically constrained source model. Any EEG activity is projected onto the cortical surface even when it may originate from deeper structures — common in epilepsy — so the reconstruction can conserve the correct overall energy while still misplacing it, distorting the virtual intracranial signal at deeper channels. Modelling deeper sources would require an orientation-free source model, which in turn would require the connectivity structure to encode each source's preferred orientation — a capability that does not yet exist, to our knowledge. One possible route forward would be to inform voxel orientations directly from tractography, but we leave this for future work. As it stands, connectivity-informed source reconstruction remains limited to fixed source orientations.

# Conclusion

Source reconstruction methods are conventionally benchmarked on their ability to localize a single, focal generator — a criterion that says little about whether a method also captures the distributed, network-level dynamics that connectivity-informed approaches are specifically designed to recover. We introduced wCSET, which replaces CSET's L1 sparsity prior with a smooth, exponentially decaying L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum, and evaluated it — together with CSET, three standard connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based (Laplace-Beltrami) alternative — against three independent ground truths for network-level activity: simulated propagation across a real structural connectome, the resected epileptogenic zone in a seizure-free clinical cohort, and simultaneous intracranial recordings.

Across all three, wCSET matched standard methods at localizing a source's focal onset, but reconstructed its subsequent spread substantially better — significantly outperforming every connectivity-agnostic competitor, and edging out CSET as well, in simulation; requiring markedly less reconstructed cortex than any other method to reach the resected zone in the clinical cohort; and, against real intracranial recordings, outperforming sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET in one of the two subjects where a scalp-visible spike made the comparison possible. This advantage proved robust: it survived considerable sensor noise, and it survived substantial degradation of the connectome itself, remaining significant through 70–80% random rewiring of its edges and never reversing outright even under full permutation. It also persisted when the true, subject-specific connectome was replaced with simple surrogates built without any diffusion MRI at all, indicating that the gain rests on coarse, large-scale connectome structure rather than on precise, individually measured tractography.

The clearest limit on this picture came from the geometry-based Beltrami alternative, which tracked wCSET more closely than any other competitor throughout, and eventually overtook it: a Beltrami-derived surrogate connectome matched, and slightly exceeded, the true connectome's own accuracy within wCSET in simulation; a full Beltrami-based variant came closest to wCSET's performance in the resection cohort, though it still needed more reconstructed cortex to reach the resection; and against real intracranial recordings, that same variant significantly outperformed wCSET on at least one metric in both evaluable subjects. Rather than undercutting the case for connectivity-informed reconstruction, this progression sharpens the open question it raises: whether it is a subject's own long-range white-matter connections, or simply the coarse, low-frequency structure that geometry and connectomics largely agree on, that drives accurate distributed source reconstruction — a question earlier, localization-only validations had no way to even pose.

Beyond wCSET itself, we see the three-part validation framework introduced here — simulated, resected, and intracranial ground truths, jointly probing a source's full activity pattern rather than its peak alone — as this work's more durable contribution. Applying it to future connectivity- and geometry-informed methods, and extending the underlying source model to represent deep and multi-generator activity beyond the fixed-orientation cortical surface used here, are natural next steps toward source imaging that reflects the brain's network organization instead of collapsing it back to a single point.
